newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian workers in anti-government "liars march".
newsitem.headline: Belgian workers in anti-government "liars march".

text.p: Thousands of Belgian workers took to the streets of the southern regional capital of Namur on Saturday to protest at what they said were politicians' lies and double-speak on jobs.

Wearing long false noses and led by a "lie detector", the protesters, dressed in traditional red and green union garb and waving flags and banners, passed peacefully by the seat of the Walloon government, the focus of their anger.

The noisy march was led by employees of bankrupt steel maker Forges de Clabecq, which folded in January when the government -- under pressure from the European Commission -- baulked at a request from administrators for fresh aid.
A banner carried by workers' wives accused Wallonia and the banks of having abandoned the company. Another said: "European Union (equals) capitalism, social exclusion and slavery."

Many local retailers closed for the day, fearful of a repeat of events in March when Clabecq workers and police clashed as protesters blocked the Paris-Brussels motorway. A jobs protest in central Brussels on Friday also turned violent.

In the event the Namur March Against the Liars passed peacefully despite an abundance of firecrackers. Many of the workers were joined by wives and children, and families easily outnumbered extremists.
Police water cannon were kept at a distance and barbed wire baricades were absent so as not to provoke outrage.
Some shops closed in sympathy with the workers' plight. "If there are no jobs, there's no purchasing power and no economy. Zero," a shop owner told RTBF television on Friday.

FGTB Clabecq union leader Roberto D'Orazio told marchers the protest was about "guaranteeing a future for the generation that follows us" and called on all workers to down tools in a national strike to defend jobs and the future of the country.
The general strike would address the federal government's pledge to tackle the country's 13 percent unemployment rate. "500,000 jobless. How did we get here?" another placard said.
Delegations from Renault Belgium, Volkswagen, Sabena, Cockerill Sambre, national railways and Caterpillar Belgium joined the Clabecq workers.

More than 3,000 Renault Belgium workers are fighting a decision by the French company to close their factory in July. Staff at airline Sabena, steel maker Cockerill, mechanical digger maker Caterpillar and the railways also face redundancies or early retirement because of restructuring plans.
"This is not a demonstration for Clabecq but against the liars...one for jobs," D'Orazio told Reuters.

Protestors accused politicians of pledging to protect jobs yet creating unemployment, promising to safeguard social security but instead undermining it with spending cuts, and of lining their own pockets.
However, in what was perhaps a sign that the protests are beginning to wane, police estimated that only 8,000 people had turned up for Saturday's demonstration.
D'Orazio said there had been 25,000 to 30,000 -- still well short of the 100,000 that organisers had hoped for.

The Namur demonstration was the fifth major jobs march in two months. A march in Brussels on March 16 led by Renault unions attracted over 50,000 workers from across Europe. About 40,000 mainly Belgian workers took part in a march in Tubize, Clabecq's home town, on February 2.
